beats.caption: The controller is the processor inside every SSD
beats.text: Between the server's PCIe link and the NAND packages sits one chip: the controller. It turns simple host commands like 'read block 7' into the exact die, plane and page operations flash needs.

beats.caption: Opened up: PHYs, CPU cores, ECC and channel engines
beats.text: The die holds a PCIe/NVMe front end, several Arm-class CPU cores, a DRAM controller, an error-correction engine and 8 to 16 flash-channel PHYs round the edge. Data-center controllers are built on 7 to 12 nm logic.

beats.caption: The FTL maps every logical block to a physical page
beats.text: Flash cannot overwrite in place, so the flash translation layer writes new data to a fresh page and updates a map. The map, about 1 GB of DRAM per TB of flash, lives in the DRAM cache beside the controller.

beats.caption: LDPC error correction cleans every read
beats.text: Cells storing 3 or 4 bits drift, so raw reads come back with errors. The LDPC engine fixes them on the fly using parity stored with each page; stronger ECC lets makers use denser, cheaper NAND.

beats.caption: Wear leveling spreads writes; that sets endurance
beats.text: Each block survives a few thousand erase cycles, so the controller rotates writes across all blocks and moves cold data. Merchant controllers: Marvell (MRVL), Silicon Motion (SIMO), Phison (8299.TWO); Samsung (005930.KS) builds its own.
